lesson.title: Step Over, Step Into, Step Out: Walking Through Code Line by Line
lesson.summary: Stepping lets you advance a paused program one line, one call, or one return at a time, using step over, step into, and step out to control how closely you follow a function's internals.
lesson.body:
Once a breakpoint has paused your program, you are not stuck looking at just that one line. Stepping lets you move forward through the code in controlled increments, watching variables and control flow change in real time, rather than jumping to the next breakpoint or letting the program run to completion.

Debuggers generally offer three stepping commands, and choosing the right one matters. Step over executes the current line completely, including any function it calls, and then pauses on the next line in the current function, without showing you what happened inside that call. Use this when you trust the function being called, perhaps because it is a well tested library function or a helper you already verified, and you do not need to watch its internals. Step into does the opposite: if the current line calls a function, step into pauses at the first line inside that function, letting you trace through its logic in detail. Use this when you suspect the bug is inside that function. Step out finishes executing the rest of the current function automatically and pauses right after it returns to whichever function called it. Use this once you have seen enough inside a function and want to get back to the bigger picture without stepping through every remaining line one by one.

Return to the recursive Fibonacci bug from the debugger tools chapter, where fib(n - 2) was mistakenly written as fib(n - 1) twice. With a breakpoint set at the first line of fib(), you run fib(4) and it pauses immediately with n equal to 4. Since the bug is suspected to be in the recursive logic itself, you step into the first recursive call, fib(n - 1), which pauses again with n now equal to 3. You keep stepping into, watching n go from 4 to 3 to 2 to 1, at which point the base case n <= 1 triggers and the function returns 1 instead of recursing further. Now you step out, watching the return value of 1 travel back up to the call with n equal to 2, which is waiting to add it to a second recursive call. You step into that second call, and here is where the bug surfaces: instead of pausing with n equal to 0, as it would if the code correctly called fib(n - 2), it pauses with n still equal to 1, because the code actually calls fib(n - 1) again. Watching that value fail to decrease the way you expected, in real time, is far more direct than trying to infer it from a pile of print output collected after the fact.

Stepping is slower than simply running to the next breakpoint, which is exactly the point: it trades speed for visibility, letting you watch the exact moment where the program's actual behavior diverges from what you expected.
